query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of silver (≈1–2 at.%) to the high-entropy alloy will promote the in-situ formation of a lubricious, Ag-rich surface film during use, thereby reducing both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate across a wide service temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline high-entropy alloy (e.g., a refractory or self‐lubricating HEA like AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5) with its standard microstructure and without any silver enrichment.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor silver content (approximately 1–2 atomic percent) during alloy synthesis so that silver is available to segregate during service.
generation.conditions: The alloy must operate under sliding or reciprocating wear conditions in environments ranging from room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures (e.g., up to 600 °C) where silver remains solid and does not evaporate or oxidize adversely.
generation.structural_mediator: The silver is expected to form nanoprecipitates that segregate to grain boundaries and surfaces, developing a continuous Ag-rich layer at contact interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Because silver has a low shear strength, its segregation to the sliding interfaces will create a lubricious tribofilm, which reduces asperity interlocking and local stress concentrations, thereby decreasing friction and wear compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated high-entropy alloy, the Ag-doped version is predicted to exhibit a lower coefficient of friction (potentially reduced by roughly 30–50%) and a significantly lower wear rate (possibly by an order of magnitude) over the specified temperature range.
generation.baseline: Wear tests and friction measurements for the untreated alloy (e.g., as reported in HEA film studies such as PMC7304825, which show COF values around 0.25 at room temperature and higher wear rates) serve as the performance baseline.
generation.boundary: This effect should remain effective as long as operating temperatures remain well below the melting or rapid oxidation temperature of Ag, and the environment does not aggressively remove or oxidize the Ag-rich tribofilm.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements (e.g., the percentage reduction in COF and wear rate) and the long-term stability of the Ag-rich layer under extended cyclic loading remain uncertain and require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one with the standard composition and one doped with 1–2 at.% Ag. Process both sets under identical synthesis and heat-treatment conditions. Subject the samples to reciprocating sliding wear tests across a temperature range (e.g., 25 °C, 300 °C, and 600 °C) under controlled load and environment. Use surface analysis techniques (e.g., SEM, EDS) to assess the formation of the Ag-rich tribofilm.
measurements: Coefficient of friction using a tribometer
Wear rate determined by mass loss and profile measurements
Surface film characterization via microscopy and compositional analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ag-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >20% reduction) in both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across the test temperatures—in comparison to the untreated alloy—the hypothesis that silver doping imparts self-lubricating improvements is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening.
